- When sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., >0.5) and forecast is rising sharply, reduce overshoot by 10–15% to avoid overcorrection.  
- If recent history shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive downward moves), model should not overpredict recovery; cap upward bias at 5% above recent low.  
- After a spike in price (e.g., >10% from prior peak), forecast should not immediately revert to prior levels — allow 1–2 days of lagged momentum before adjusting.  
- If sentiment is negative (e.g., < -0.5) and forecast is still rising, reduce forecast slope by 20–30% to reflect bearish sentiment.  
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome deviates >10% from 14-day moving average, adjust forecast to align with recent trend, not just historical mean.  
- When sentiment flips from negative to positive mid-horizon, model should not jump 5%+ above prior peak — cap upward movement at 3–5% unless confirmed by new event.  
- If true outcome shows sharp drop after forecast peak, assume model overestimated momentum — reduce next period’s forecast by 5–10% to reflect “reversal lag.”
